query: What is the governance procedure in force and its latest version regulating the suitability and composition of a credit institution's management body?
answer:
The governance procedures in force regulating the suitability and composition of a credit institution's management body are:

## Primary Governance Procedures

**1. Joint ESMA and EBA Guidelines on the Assessment of the Suitability of Members of the Management Body and Key Function Holders (EBA/GL/2021/06)**

This is the latest version of the guidelines specifically addressing suitability and composition, issued in 2021 by the European Banking Authority (EBA) and the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA).

**Key provisions include:**
- Eligibility criteria requiring members of the management body and key function holders to be of good repute and possess adequate knowledge, skills and experience
- Scope covering banks, credit institutions, investment firms (all classes), third-country branches and financial holding companies
- Assessment process requiring institutions to carry out suitability assessments before appointment and on an ongoing basis; competent authorities may also assess suitability
- Compliance and reporting obligations requiring institutions to keep records of assessments and report suitability results to the competent authority
- Time-commitment expectations specifying the annual time commitment expected from each member
- Directorship-counting obligations for compliance with Article 91(3) CRD
- Induction and training requirements: newly appointed members must receive induction within one month and complete training within six months covering ICT-related risks, ESG factors, AI technologies, and diversity
- Mapping of duties requiring institutions to map duties and provide individual statements on responsibilities of each member
- Individual suitability assessment covering reputation, experience, governance criteria (including conflicts of interest and time commitment)
- Collective suitability requirement: the management body as a whole must possess adequate collective knowledge, skills, and experience relevant to the institution's business model, strategy, risk appetite, and activities
- Diversity emphasis: gender-balanced composition is emphasized, and institutions must develop diversity policies
- AML/CTF knowledge: at least one management body member must be responsible for AML implementation, and all members must understand AML/TF risks
- Ongoing monitoring: significant institutions must conduct individual and collective suitability assessments at least annually; less significant institutions at least every two years

**2. EBA Guidelines on Internal Governance (EBA/GL/2021/05)**

This is the latest version issued in 2021, specifying internal governance arrangements, processes, and mechanisms that credit institutions must implement under Article 74(1) of Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD IV/V).

**Key provisions include:**
- Documented roles and duties for each management body member, senior manager, and key function holder
- Requirements for gender diversity and balance in the composition of management bodies
- Individual statements of responsibility for management body members
- A holistic risk management framework subject to independent review
- Oversight of financial reporting integrity and internal control frameworks
- Alignment with CRD VI and the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA)
- Third-country branches guidance ensuring robust governance frameworks
- Management body responsibilities with enhanced clarity on supervisory and management functions, and conflicts of interest
- Outsourcing arrangements including governance frameworks, due diligence on service providers, and establishment of registers for outsourcing agreements
- Credit institutions must assign at least every three years a review and evaluation of the composition, efficiency, and effectiveness of the management body and its committees to an independent external consultant

## Legal Basis

**Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD IV/V), particularly Article 91**, establishes the legal requirements that members of the management body of a credit institution must meet, including sufficient knowledge, skills, and experience, as well as honesty, integrity, and independence of mind.

**Directive 2014/65/EU (MiFID II)** extends similar corporate governance requirements to investment firms.

## Assessment Procedure

- Credit institutions must assess suitability of management body members prior to appointment and on an ongoing basis, using defined criteria on reputation, experience, and governance
- Competent authorities (e.g., the ECB for significant institutions, national authorities for less significant ones) conduct their own suitability assessments and may refuse authorisation if members do not meet the requirements
- The management body must reflect the knowledge, skills, and experience necessary to fulfil its responsibilities, including understanding of the institution's business, main risks, risk management, financial reporting, and regulatory requirements
- The management body has ultimate and overall responsibility for the credit institution and must define, oversee, and be accountable for governance arrangements ensuring effective and prudent management
- Institutions must have a suitable and transparent organisational and operational structure with effective reporting lines and allocation of responsibilities

## Latest Developments

In February 2026, the EBA and ESMA launched a new consultation on revised joint guidelines on the assessment of suitability of management body members and key function holders, forming part of a broader "Suitability Package" that also includes draft Regulatory Technical Standards (RTS) on documentation requirements for large institutions. The consultation closed on 25 May 2026. The revisions cover proportionality, diversity, reputation, skills, training, and ongoing monitoring requirements.

The EU regulatory framework establishes detailed governance procedures for assessing the **suitability** and **composition** of the management body of credit institutions. The key instruments are:

### 1. Legal Basis

- **Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD IV/V)**, particularly **Article 91**, sets out the requirements that members of the management body of a credit institution must meet, including sufficient knowledge, skills, and experience, as well as honesty, integrity, and independence of mind.
- **Directive 2014/65/EU (MiFID II)** extends similar corporate governance requirements to investment firms.

### 2. Key EU Guidelines

- **EBA Guidelines on Internal Governance (EBA/GL/2021/05)**: Issued in 2021, these guidelines specify the internal governance arrangements, processes, and mechanisms that credit institutions must implement under Article 74(1) of the CRD. Key provisions include:
  - Documented roles and duties for each management body member, senior manager, and key function holder.
  - Requirements for gender diversity and balance in the composition of management bodies.
  - Individual statements of responsibility for management body members.
  - A holistic risk management framework subject to independent review.
  - Oversight of financial reporting integrity and internal control frameworks.
  - Alignment with CRD VI and the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA).

- **Joint ESMA and EBA Guidelines on the Assessment of the Suitability of Members of the Management Body and Key Function Holders (EBA/GL/2021/06)**: These guidelines specify the criteria and processes for assessing suitability, covering:
  - **Individual suitability**: Reputation, experience, governance criteria (including conflicts of interest and time commitment).
  - **Collective suitability**: The management body as a whole must possess adequate collective knowledge, skills, and experience relevant to the institution's business model, strategy, risk appetite, and activities.
  - **Diversity**: Gender-balanced composition is emphasised, and institutions must develop diversity policies.
  - **AML/CTF knowledge**: At least one management body member must be responsible for AML implementation, and all members must understand AML/TF risks.
  - **Ongoing monitoring**: Significant institutions must conduct individual and collective suitability assessments at least annually; less significant institutions at least every two years.

### 3. Assessment Procedure

- **Credit institutions** must assess suitability of management body members prior to appointment and on an ongoing basis, using defined criteria on reputation, experience, and governance.
- **Competent authorities** (e.g., the ECB for significant institutions, national authorities for less significant ones) conduct their own suitability assessments and may refuse authorisation if members do not meet the requirements.
- Credit institutions must assign at least every **three years** a review and evaluation of the composition, efficiency, and effectiveness of the management body and its committees to an **independent external consultant**.

### 4. Composition Requirements

- The management body must reflect the knowledge, skills, and experience necessary to fulfil its responsibilities, including understanding of the institution's business, main risks, risk management, financial reporting, and regulatory requirements.
- The management body has ultimate and overall responsibility for the credit institution and must define, oversee, and be accountable for governance arrangements ensuring effective and prudent management.
- Institutions must have a suitable and transparent organisational and operational structure with effective reporting lines and allocation of responsibilities.

### 5. Latest Developments

In **February 2026**, the EBA and ESMA launched a new consultation on revised joint guidelines on the assessment of suitability of management body members and key function holders, forming part of a broader **"Suitability Package"** that also includes draft Regulatory Technical Standards (RTS) on documentation requirements for large institutions. The consultation closed on 25 May 2026. The revisions cover proportionality, diversity, reputation, skills, training, and ongoing monitoring requirements.

## Governance Procedures for Suitability and Composition of the Management Body of Credit Institutions

The EU regulatory framework establishes detailed governance procedures for assessing the **suitability** and **composition** of the management body of credit institutions. The key instruments are:

### 1. Legal Basis

- **Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD IV/V)**, particularly **Article 91**, sets out the requirements that members of the management body of a credit institution must meet, including sufficient knowledge, skills, and experience, as well as honesty, integrity, and independence of mind.
- **Directive 2014/65/EU (MiFID II)** extends similar corporate governance requirements to investment firms.

### 2. Key EU Guidelines

- **EBA Guidelines on Internal Governance (EBA/GL/2021/05)**: Issued in 2021, these guidelines specify the internal governance arrangements, processes, and mechanisms that credit institutions must implement under Article 74(1) of the CRD. Key provisions include:
  - Documented roles and duties for each management body member, senior manager, and key function holder.
  - Requirements for gender diversity and balance in the composition of management bodies.
  - Individual statements of responsibility for management body members.
  - A holistic risk management framework subject to independent review.
  - Oversight of financial reporting integrity and internal control frameworks.
  - Alignment with CRD VI and the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA).

- **Joint ESMA and EBA Guidelines on the Assessment of the Suitability of Members of the Management Body and Key Function Holders (EBA/GL/2021/06)**: These guidelines specify the criteria and processes for assessing suitability, covering:
  - **Individual suitability**: Reputation, experience, governance criteria (including conflicts of interest and time commitment).
  - **Collective suitability**: The management body as a whole must possess adequate collective knowledge, skills, and experience relevant to the institution's business model, strategy, risk appetite, and activities.
  - **Diversity**: Gender-balanced composition is emphasised, and institutions must develop diversity policies.
  - **AML/CTF knowledge**: At least one management body member must be responsible for AML implementation, and all members must understand AML/TF risks.
  - **Ongoing monitoring**: Significant institutions must conduct individual and collective suitability assessments at least annually; less significant institutions at least every two years.

### 3. Assessment Procedure

- **Credit institutions** must assess suitability of management body members prior to appointment and on an ongoing basis, using defined criteria on reputation, experience, and governance.
- **Competent authorities** (e.g., the ECB for significant institutions, national authorities for less significant ones) conduct their own suitability assessments and may refuse authorisation if members do not meet the requirements.
- Credit institutions must assign at least every **three years** a review and evaluation of the composition, efficiency, and effectiveness of the management body and its committees to an **independent external consultant**.

### 4. Composition Requirements

- The management body must reflect the knowledge, skills, and experience necessary to fulfil its responsibilities, including understanding of the institution's business, main risks, risk management, financial reporting, and regulatory requirements.
- The management body has ultimate and overall responsibility for the credit institution and must define, oversee, and be accountable for governance arrangements ensuring effective and prudent management.
- Institutions must have a suitable and transparent organisational and operational structure with effective reporting lines and allocation of responsibilities.

### 5. Latest Developments

In **February 2026**, the EBA and ESMA launched a new consultation on revised joint guidelines on the assessment of suitability of management body members and key function holders, forming part of a broader **"Suitability Package"** that also includes draft Regulatory Technical Standards (RTS) on documentation requirements for large institutions. The consultation closed on 25 May 2026. The revisions cover proportionality, diversity, reputation, skills, training, and ongoing monitoring requirements.

explainability.content: Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD IV/V) Article 91 requires management body members to have sufficient knowledge, skills, experience, honesty, integrity and independence, establishing the legal basis for suitability requirements.

EBA Guidelines on Internal Governance (EBA/GL/2021/05) detail documented roles, duties and individual statements of responsibility for each management body member, senior manager and key function holder, supporting the procedural implementation of the legal basis.

Joint ESMA‑EBA Guidelines (EBA/GL/2021/06) specify the criteria for individual suitability – reputation, experience, governance criteria, time‑commitment and conflicts of interest – and require credit institutions to assess these before appointment and on an ongoing basis.

The same joint guidelines require collective suitability, meaning the management body as a whole must possess adequate knowledge, skills and experience relevant to the institution’s business model, strategy, risk appetite and activities.
Both guidelines emphasise gender‑balanced composition and the need for a diversity policy, aligning with the EBA internal‑governance guideline’s provision on gender diversity.

The guidelines mandate that at least one management body member be responsible for AML/CTF implementation and that all members understand AML/TF risks, linking suitability to anti‑money‑laundering competence.
Credit institutions must conduct suitability assessments at least annually for significant institutions and every two years for less‑significant ones, as set out in the joint guidelines.

Competent authorities (ECB for significant institutions, national authorities for others) perform their own suitability assessments and may refuse authorisation if members do not meet the requirements, reflecting the procedural role of authorities.

Credit institutions must review the composition, efficiency and effectiveness of the management body every three years by an independent external consultant, as required by the internal‑governance guideline.

input.answer:
The governance procedures in force regulating the suitability and composition of a credit institution's management body are:

## Primary Governance Procedures

**1. Joint ESMA and EBA Guidelines on the Assessment of the Suitability of Members of the Management Body and Key Function Holders (EBA/GL/2021/06)**

This is the latest version of the guidelines specifically addressing suitability and composition, issued in 2021 by the European Banking Authority (EBA) and the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA).

**Key provisions include:**
- Eligibility criteria requiring members of the management body and key function holders to be of good repute and possess adequate knowledge, skills and experience
- Scope covering banks, credit institutions, investment firms (all classes), third-country branches and financial holding companies
- Assessment process requiring institutions to carry out suitability assessments before appointment and on an ongoing basis; competent authorities may also assess suitability
- Compliance and reporting obligations requiring institutions to keep records of assessments and report suitability results to the competent authority
- Time-commitment expectations specifying the annual time commitment expected from each member
- Directorship-counting obligations for compliance with Article 91(3) CRD
- Induction and training requirements: newly appointed members must receive induction within one month and complete training within six months covering ICT-related risks, ESG factors, AI technologies, and diversity
- Mapping of duties requiring institutions to map duties and provide individual statements on responsibilities of each member
- Individual suitability assessment covering reputation, experience, governance criteria (including conflicts of interest and time commitment)
- Collective suitability requirement: the management body as a whole must possess adequate collective knowledge, skills, and experience relevant to the institution's business model, strategy, risk appetite, and activities
- Diversity emphasis: gender-balanced composition is emphasized, and institutions must develop diversity policies
- AML/CTF knowledge: at least one management body member must be responsible for AML implementation, and all members must understand AML/TF risks
- Ongoing monitoring: significant institutions must conduct individual and collective suitability assessments at least annually; less significant institutions at least every two years

**2. EBA Guidelines on Internal Governance (EBA/GL/2021/05)**

This is the latest version issued in 2021, specifying internal governance arrangements, processes, and mechanisms that credit institutions must implement under Article 74(1) of Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD IV/V).

**Key provisions include:**
- Documented roles and duties for each management body member, senior manager, and key function holder
- Requirements for gender diversity and balance in the composition of management bodies
- Individual statements of responsibility for management body members
- A holistic risk management framework subject to independent review
- Oversight of financial reporting integrity and internal control frameworks
- Alignment with CRD VI and the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA)
- Third-country branches guidance ensuring robust governance frameworks
- Management body responsibilities with enhanced clarity on supervisory and management functions, and conflicts of interest
- Outsourcing arrangements including governance frameworks, due diligence on service providers, and establishment of registers for outsourcing agreements
- Credit institutions must assign at least every three years a review and evaluation of the composition, efficiency, and effectiveness of the management body and its committees to an independent external consultant

## Legal Basis

**Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD IV/V), particularly Article 91**, establishes the legal requirements that members of the management body of a credit institution must meet, including sufficient knowledge, skills, and experience, as well as honesty, integrity, and independence of mind.

**Directive 2014/65/EU (MiFID II)** extends similar corporate governance requirements to investment firms.

## Assessment Procedure

- Credit institutions must assess suitability of management body members prior to appointment and on an ongoing basis, using defined criteria on reputation, experience, and governance
- Competent authorities (e.g., the ECB for significant institutions, national authorities for less significant ones) conduct their own suitability assessments and may refuse authorisation if members do not meet the requirements
- The management body must reflect the knowledge, skills, and experience necessary to fulfil its responsibilities, including understanding of the institution's business, main risks, risk management, financial reporting, and regulatory requirements
- The management body has ultimate and overall responsibility for the credit institution and must define, oversee, and be accountable for governance arrangements ensuring effective and prudent management
- Institutions must have a suitable and transparent organisational and operational structure with effective reporting lines and allocation of responsibilities

## Latest Developments

In February 2026, the EBA and ESMA launched a new consultation on revised joint guidelines on the assessment of suitability of management body members and key function holders, forming part of a broader "Suitability Package" that also includes draft Regulatory Technical Standards (RTS) on documentation requirements for large institutions. The consultation closed on 25 May 2026. The revisions cover proportionality, diversity, reputation, skills, training, and ongoing monitoring requirements.

query: What are the key takeaways of CEOE reports affecting the financial sector?
answer:
## Key Takeaways of CEOE Reports Affecting the Financial Sector

The **Confederación Española de Organizaciones Empresariales (CEOE)**, Spain's leading employers' organization founded in 1977, engages with the financial sector through various channels and initiatives. While specific standalone CEOE reports exclusively focused on the financial sector were not identified, CEOE's engagement with financial sector issues is channeled through its economic commissions, policy advocacy, and participation in multi-stakeholder initiatives. Here are the key takeaways:

### Organizational Structure for Financial Sector Engagement

- **Comisión de Economía y Política Financiera de la CEOE**: A dedicated commission focused on economic and financial policy matters
- **Departamento de Economía, Servicio de Estudios (CEOE)**: The economics department and research service that produces economic analyses and reports
- **Member organizations**: Financial-sector organizations such as the **Confederación Española de Cajas de Ahorro (CECA)** are members, linking savings banks to the CEOE umbrella

### Key Financial Sector Issues and Policy Positions

**1. BBVA-Sabadell Merger**
- CEOE President Antonio Garamendi publicly urged the Spanish government to make a swift decision on the proposed BBVA takeover of Sabadell, highlighting the implications for Spain's banking sector

**2. Financial Sector Reform**
- The Spanish government faces a legislative backlog on several laws to reform the financial sector
- Key priority: establishment of the **Autoridad del Cliente Financiero** (Financial Customer Authority) before year-end

**3. Financial Inclusion**
- The Spanish banking sector has reported progress on financial inclusion
- Over 70,000 residents in 79 rural municipalities gained physical access to financial services
- CEOE participates in broader observatories and initiatives alongside entities like CEPYME on issues affecting consumers and businesses

**4. Energy Costs Impacting Business Financial Performance**
- CEOE is part of an observatory (alongside Aelec, ACIE, CEPYME, and others) that has flagged rising electricity system operation costs
- Estimated accumulated costs: **€3,850 million in 2026**
- These costs directly affect the financial performance of companies across sectors
- Impact breakdown:
  - 7% impact on domestic consumer bills
  - 10% impact on SME bills
  - 15% impact on energy-intensive industries

### Economic Context

Spain's macroeconomic conditions form the backdrop for CEOE's policy positions on financial regulation and business competitiveness:
- **GDP growth**: 2.7% year-on-year in Q2 2026
- **Full-year 2026 forecast**: 2.5% GDP growth
- **Inflation projection**: 3.2% for 2026

### Summary

CEOE's financial-sector engagement is primarily channeled through its economic commissions, policy advocacy on major banking sector developments (such as the BBVA-Sabadell merger), participation in financial inclusion initiatives, and advocacy on cross-cutting issues like energy costs that affect business financial performance. The organization represents around two million companies and self-employed workers across all sectors through a network of more than 200 territorial and sectoral business associations.

## CEOE and the Financial Sector

The **Confederación Española de Organizaciones Empresariales (CEOE)** is Spain's leading employers' organization, founded in 1977. It represents around two million companies and self-employed workers across all sectors through a network of more than 200 territorial and sectoral business associations.

### CEOE's engagement with the financial sector

CEOE has several bodies and activities relevant to the financial sector:

- **Comisión de Economía y Política Financiera de la CEOE** — a dedicated commission focused on economic and financial policy matters.
- **Departamento de Economía, Servicio de Estudios (CEOE)** — the economics department and research service that produces economic analyses and reports.
- Among its members are financial-sector organizations such as the **Confederación Española de Cajas de Ahorro (CECA)**, linking savings banks to the CEOE umbrella.

### Key financial-sector topics involving CEOE

- **BBVA-Sabadell merger**: CEOE President Antonio Garamendi publicly urged the Spanish government to make a swift decision on the proposed BBVA takeover of Sabadell, highlighting the implications for Spain's banking sector.
- **Financial sector reform**: The Spanish government faces a legislative backlog on several laws to reform the financial sector, including the establishment of the *Autoridad del Cliente Financiero* (Financial Customer Authority) before year-end.
- **Financial inclusion**: The Spanish banking sector has reported progress on financial inclusion, with over 70,000 residents in 79 rural municipalities gaining physical access to financial services. CEOE participates in broader observatories and initiatives alongside entities like CEPYME on issues affecting consumers and businesses.
- **Energy costs impacting businesses**: CEOE is part of an observatory (alongside Aelec, ACIE, CEPYME, and others) that has flagged rising electricity system operation costs — estimated at €3,850 million accumulated in 2026 — which directly affect the financial performance of companies across sectors.

### Economic outlook context

Spain's economy has shown resilience in 2026, with GDP growth of 2.7% year-on-year in Q2 2026 and forecasts revised upward to 2.5% for the full year. Inflation is projected at 3.2% for 2026. These macroeconomic conditions form the backdrop for CEOE's policy positions on financial regulation and business competitiveness.

*Note: Specific standalone CEOE reports exclusively focused on the financial sector were not identified in available sources. CEOE's financial-sector engagement is primarily channeled through its economic commissions, policy advocacy, and participation in multi-stakeholder initiatives.*

The banking sector has reported progress on financial inclusion, with over 70,000 residents in 79 rural municipalities gaining physical access to financial services.

CEOE participates in an observatory that flagged rising electricity system‑operation costs—estimated at €3,850 million in 2026—which directly affect the financial performance of companies across sectors.

Spain’s macro‑economic context in 2026 shows GDP growth of 2.7% YoY in Q2 and an inflation forecast of 3.2%, providing the backdrop for CEOE’s policy positions on financial regulation and competitiveness.

Según el informe del Servicio de Estudios de la Cámara de España, publicado este 15 de septiembre en Madrid, la economía nacional ha demostrado una «notable capacidad de resistencia». El PIB registró un crecimiento interanual del 2,7% en el segundo trimestre, una cifra que supera a las principales economías europeas y que se apoya en la fortaleza del consumo privado, el dinamismo de las exportaciones de servicios, con el turismo a la cabeza, y la inversión.

## La demanda nacional, pilar del crecimiento en 2026 [...] Por su parte, la inversión mantendrá un ritmo sólido, con un crecimiento del 4,5% en 2026 y del 3,8% en 2027. La moderación del próximo año se atribuye en parte a la reducción gradual del impulso directo de los fondos Next Generation EU, cuya fase más intensa de ejecución se concentró entre 2025 y 2026.

## La inflación y el entorno internacional, principales riesgos

La inflación se mantiene como una de las variables más sensibles. La Cámara de España sitúa la media de 2026 en el 3,2%, cinco décimas por encima de su anterior previsión. Este repunte se debe al encarecimiento de alimentos y productos energéticos, así como a la retirada de las medidas extraordinarias de contención de precios. Para 2027, se espera una moderación hasta el 2,4%. [...] La Cámara de Comercio de España ha revisado al alza su previsión de crecimiento para la economía española en 2026 hasta el 2,5%, dos décimas por encima de su estimación anterior. Este optimismo, basado en el dinamismo de la demanda interna durante la primera mitad del año y el efecto de arrastre, contrasta con el ajuste a la baja para 2027, que sitúa en el 1,9%, ante la complejidad del escenario internacional.

## Key Takeaways of CEOE Reports Affecting the Financial Sector

The **Confederación Española de Organizaciones Empresariales (CEOE)**, Spain's leading employers' organization founded in 1977, engages with the financial sector through various channels and initiatives. While specific standalone CEOE reports exclusively focused on the financial sector were not identified, CEOE's engagement with financial sector issues is channeled through its economic commissions, policy advocacy, and participation in multi-stakeholder initiatives. Here are the key takeaways:

### Organizational Structure for Financial Sector Engagement

- **Comisión de Economía y Política Financiera de la CEOE**: A dedicated commission focused on economic and financial policy matters
- **Departamento de Economía, Servicio de Estudios (CEOE)**: The economics department and research service that produces economic analyses and reports
- **Member organizations**: Financial-sector organizations such as the **Confederación Española de Cajas de Ahorro (CECA)** are members, linking savings banks to the CEOE umbrella

### Key Financial Sector Issues and Policy Positions

**1. BBVA-Sabadell Merger**
- CEOE President Antonio Garamendi publicly urged the Spanish government to make a swift decision on the proposed BBVA takeover of Sabadell, highlighting the implications for Spain's banking sector

**2. Financial Sector Reform**
- The Spanish government faces a legislative backlog on several laws to reform the financial sector
- Key priority: establishment of the **Autoridad del Cliente Financiero** (Financial Customer Authority) before year-end

**3. Financial Inclusion**
- The Spanish banking sector has reported progress on financial inclusion
- Over 70,000 residents in 79 rural municipalities gained physical access to financial services
- CEOE participates in broader observatories and initiatives alongside entities like CEPYME on issues affecting consumers and businesses

**4. Energy Costs Impacting Business Financial Performance**
- CEOE is part of an observatory (alongside Aelec, ACIE, CEPYME, and others) that has flagged rising electricity system operation costs
- Estimated accumulated costs: **€3,850 million in 2026**
- These costs directly affect the financial performance of companies across sectors
- Impact breakdown:
  - 7% impact on domestic consumer bills
  - 10% impact on SME bills
  - 15% impact on energy-intensive industries

### Economic Context

Spain's macroeconomic conditions form the backdrop for CEOE's policy positions on financial regulation and business competitiveness:
- **GDP growth**: 2.7% year-on-year in Q2 2026
- **Full-year 2026 forecast**: 2.5% GDP growth
- **Inflation projection**: 3.2% for 2026

### Summary

CEOE's financial-sector engagement is primarily channeled through its economic commissions, policy advocacy on major banking sector developments (such as the BBVA-Sabadell merger), participation in financial inclusion initiatives, and advocacy on cross-cutting issues like energy costs that affect business financial performance. The organization represents around two million companies and self-employed workers across all sectors through a network of more than 200 territorial and sectoral business associations.

query: What is the sector's stance (CECA) on banking regulation in Spain?
answer:
## CECA's Stance on Banking Regulation in Spain

**CECA** (Confederación Española de Cajas de Ahorros) is the Spanish association of savings banks and banks created by them, headquartered in Madrid. It represents and defends the interests of its member entities at both national and European levels, engaging with EU institutions in Brussels on issues including banking regulation, financial inclusion, sustainable finance, and social investment.

### Core Regulatory Positions

**1. Regulatory Simplification for Competitiveness**

CECA, together with the other main Spanish banking associations (AEB and UNACC), has been a vocal advocate for **simplifying the European banking regulatory framework** to promote economic growth and EU competitiveness. At a joint event held in Frankfurt, the three associations presented concrete simplification proposals covering financial regulation, digital affairs, and sustainability. CECA's Managing Director Antonio Romero stated: *"Simplification is not an objective in itself; it is the only way to improve European competitiveness and autonomy."*

Key proposals include:
- **Simplification of the macroprudential framework** to avoid duplication between agencies
- **Improvement of accountability** in the regulatory process and incorporation of **ex-post evaluation** of regulations
- **Regulatory proportionality** — ensuring rules are calibrated to the size and complexity of institutions
- **Reduction of the number of capital buffers** and avoidance of overlaps
- A **broader focus for regulators and supervisors**, incorporating a secondary objective of growth and competitiveness alongside financial stability

The associations estimated that regulatory simplification could increase lending by around **€250 billion in Spain alone** and over **€2 trillion across Europe**, potentially lifting euro-zone GDP by 2.7%.

**2. Completion of the Banking Union**

CECA supports completing the EU Banking Union, including the establishment of a **single European Deposit Guarantee Fund (EDIS)** and advancing the **Savings and Investment Union (SIU)**.

**3. Financial Inclusion**

CECA, AEB, and UNACC have actively worked on financial inclusion measures. According to their joint report (based on research by the Valencian Institute of Economic Research — IVIE), **99.3% of the Spanish population has access to banking services**. CECA advocates for proximity banking and measures to bridge the digital divide, particularly for elderly populations.

**4. Sustainable Finance**

CECA participates in sustainable finance initiatives and supports the EU's sustainability goals, while calling for the sustainable finance framework to remain **proportionate and competitive**. CECA's member foundations constitute the leading private social investor in Spain through their "Obra Social" programmes.

**5. Digital Regulation and Payments**

CECA co-organises events on the **Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA)** and RegTech trends, and supports the interconnection of European payment systems. Together with AEB and UNACC, CECA backs the Bizum platform's integration with 13 European countries and advocates for European sovereignty in payment systems.

**6. Academic Research on Regulation's Impact**

CECA has launched a joint academic chair with the **Pontifical University of Comillas** to promote research on the economic impact of banking regulation, aiming to provide rigorous evidence to the public debate on how regulation affects lending, competitiveness, and the real economy.

### EU-Level Engagement

CECA maintains active representation in Brussels and is affiliated with the **European Savings and Retail Banking Group (ESBG)** and the **World Savings and Retail Banking Institute (WSBI)**. It contributes position papers, participates in EU consultations, and engages with the European Banking Authority (EBA) on prudential regulation topics. During the 2023 Spanish Presidency of the EU Council, CECA published a priorities document covering solvency, sustainability, financial markets, AML/CFT, payments, digital banking, and Banking Union.

## CECA's Stance on Banking Regulation in Spain

**CECA** (Confederación Española de Cajas de Ahorros) is the Spanish association of savings banks and banks created by them. Headquartered in Madrid, it represents and defends the interests of its member entities at both national and European levels, engaging with EU institutions in Brussels on issues such as banking regulation, financial inclusion, sustainable finance, and social investment.

### Core Regulatory Positions

**1. Regulatory Simplification for Competitiveness**

CECA, together with the other main Spanish banking associations (AEB and UNACC), has been a vocal advocate for **simplifying the European banking regulatory framework** to promote economic growth and EU competitiveness. At a joint event held in Frankfurt, the three associations presented concrete simplification proposals covering financial regulation, digital affairs, and sustainability. CECA's Managing Director Antonio Romero stated: *"Simplification is not an objective in itself; it is the only way to improve European competitiveness and autonomy."*

Key proposals include:
- **Simplification of the macroprudential framework** to avoid duplication between agencies.
- **Improvement of accountability** in the regulatory process and incorporation of **ex-post evaluation** of regulations.
- **Regulatory proportionality** — ensuring rules are calibrated to the size and complexity of institutions.
- **Reduction of the number of capital buffers** and avoidance of overlaps.
- A **broader focus for regulators and supervisors**, incorporating a secondary objective of growth and competitiveness alongside financial stability.

The associations estimated that regulatory simplification could increase lending by around **€250 billion in Spain alone** and over **€2 trillion across Europe**, potentially lifting euro-zone GDP by 2.7%.

**2. Completion of the Banking Union**

CECA supports completing the EU Banking Union, including the establishment of a **single European Deposit Guarantee Fund (EDIS)** and advancing the **Savings and Investment Union (SIU)**.

**3. Financial Inclusion**

CECA, AEB, and UNACC have actively worked on financial inclusion measures. According to their joint report (based on research by the Valencian Institute of Economic Research — IVIE), **99.3% of the Spanish population has access to banking services**. CECA advocates for proximity banking and measures to bridge the digital divide, particularly for elderly populations.

**4. Sustainable Finance**

CECA participates in sustainable finance initiatives and supports the EU's sustainability goals, while calling for the sustainable finance framework to remain **proportionate and competitive**. CECA's member foundations constitute the leading private social investor in Spain through their "Obra Social" programmes.

**5. Digital Regulation and Payments**

CECA co-organises events on the **Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA)** and RegTech trends, and supports the interconnection of European payment systems. Together with AEB and UNACC, CECA backs the Bizum platform's integration with 13 European countries and advocates for European sovereignty in payment systems.

**6. Academic Research on Regulation's Impact**

CECA has launched a joint academic chair with the **Pontifical University of Comillas** to promote research on the economic impact of banking regulation, aiming to provide rigorous evidence to the public debate on how regulation affects lending, competitiveness, and the real economy.

### EU-Level Engagement

CECA maintains active representation in Brussels and is affiliated with the **European Savings and Retail Banking Group (ESBG)** and the **World Savings and Retail Banking Institute (WSBI)**. It contributes position papers, participates in EU consultations, and engages with the European Banking Authority (EBA) on prudential regulation topics. During the 2023 Spanish Presidency of the EU Council, CECA published a priorities document covering solvency, sustainability, financial markets, AML/CFT, payments, digital banking, and Banking Union.

## CECA's Stance on Banking Regulation in Spain

**CECA** (Confederación Española de Cajas de Ahorros) is the Spanish association of savings banks and banks created by them, headquartered in Madrid. It represents and defends the interests of its member entities at both national and European levels, engaging with EU institutions in Brussels on issues including banking regulation, financial inclusion, sustainable finance, and social investment.

### Core Regulatory Positions

**1. Regulatory Simplification for Competitiveness**

CECA, together with the other main Spanish banking associations (AEB and UNACC), has been a vocal advocate for **simplifying the European banking regulatory framework** to promote economic growth and EU competitiveness. At a joint event held in Frankfurt, the three associations presented concrete simplification proposals covering financial regulation, digital affairs, and sustainability. CECA's Managing Director Antonio Romero stated: *"Simplification is not an objective in itself; it is the only way to improve European competitiveness and autonomy."*

Key proposals include:
- **Simplification of the macroprudential framework** to avoid duplication between agencies
- **Improvement of accountability** in the regulatory process and incorporation of **ex-post evaluation** of regulations
- **Regulatory proportionality** — ensuring rules are calibrated to the size and complexity of institutions
- **Reduction of the number of capital buffers** and avoidance of overlaps
- A **broader focus for regulators and supervisors**, incorporating a secondary objective of growth and competitiveness alongside financial stability

The associations estimated that regulatory simplification could increase lending by around **€250 billion in Spain alone** and over **€2 trillion across Europe**, potentially lifting euro-zone GDP by 2.7%.

**2. Completion of the Banking Union**

CECA supports completing the EU Banking Union, including the establishment of a **single European Deposit Guarantee Fund (EDIS)** and advancing the **Savings and Investment Union (SIU)**.

**3. Financial Inclusion**

CECA, AEB, and UNACC have actively worked on financial inclusion measures. According to their joint report (based on research by the Valencian Institute of Economic Research — IVIE), **99.3% of the Spanish population has access to banking services**. CECA advocates for proximity banking and measures to bridge the digital divide, particularly for elderly populations.

**4. Sustainable Finance**

CECA participates in sustainable finance initiatives and supports the EU's sustainability goals, while calling for the sustainable finance framework to remain **proportionate and competitive**. CECA's member foundations constitute the leading private social investor in Spain through their "Obra Social" programmes.

**5. Digital Regulation and Payments**

CECA co-organises events on the **Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA)** and RegTech trends, and supports the interconnection of European payment systems. Together with AEB and UNACC, CECA backs the Bizum platform's integration with 13 European countries and advocates for European sovereignty in payment systems.

**6. Academic Research on Regulation's Impact**

CECA has launched a joint academic chair with the **Pontifical University of Comillas** to promote research on the economic impact of banking regulation, aiming to provide rigorous evidence to the public debate on how regulation affects lending, competitiveness, and the real economy.

### EU-Level Engagement

CECA maintains active representation in Brussels and is affiliated with the **European Savings and Retail Banking Group (ESBG)** and the **World Savings and Retail Banking Institute (WSBI)**. It contributes position papers, participates in EU consultations, and engages with the European Banking Authority (EBA) on prudential regulation topics. During the 2023 Spanish Presidency of the EU Council, CECA published a priorities document covering solvency, sustainability, financial markets, AML/CFT, payments, digital banking, and Banking Union.

query: What is the public market outlook and the sector and competitor signals in financial services per the consultancy's latest report?
answer:
**Public Market Outlook and Sector/Competitor Signals in Financial Services per Latest Consultancy Reports**

## Public Market Outlook

**Macroeconomic Pressure on Banks**
Deloitte's 2026 *Banking and Capital Markets Outlook* warns that macroeconomic uncertainty, divergent consumer sentiment, and persistent inflation could test U.S. banks' revenues and profitability, even though strong capital positions provide resilience. The report indicates that banks will need to defend margins, diversify fee income, and prepare for heightened competition from non-bank entities. Tokenized deposits are highlighted as a possible counter-measure to stablecoin-related funding pressures.

**UK Public M&A Activity**
The latest public market update shows that M&A activity is especially pronounced in the UK financial services sector, with many $5 billion-plus transactions and activity levels not seen since 2018. Deals are being driven by corporates, private equity firms, and overseas acquirers, signaling strong competitive tension in the sector.

**Deal Flow Acceleration**
Lincoln International reports a material increase in signed engagement letters and a pick-up in M&A deal flow as private equity investment backlogs melt and retail money fuels demand for greater valuation transparency. The firm links this surge in deal flow to stronger business momentum and a robust public market, reinforcing the view of accelerating activity in the sector.

## Sector and Competitor Signals

**Heightened Competition from Non-Bank Entities**
Banks face increased competition from non-bank entities, requiring them to defend margins and diversify fee income streams to maintain relevance and profitability.

**Tokenization as Competitive Imperative**
A joint Oliver Wyman and UK Finance report stresses that the UK must act urgently on securities tokenization to stay globally competitive. The report estimates the global tokenized market could reach **$2 trillion by 2030**. It warns that the UK is lagging behind other jurisdictions, creating a competitive risk for domestic financial services firms if the market is not accelerated.

**Tokenized Deposits vs. Stablecoins**
Deloitte's report notes tokenized deposits as a counter-strategy for banks concerned about stablecoin funding pressures, underscoring the competitive pressure from emerging digital asset players. Unlike stablecoins, tokenized deposits remain within the existing regulatory framework of a bank, subject to the same capital management and regulatory oversight.

**Cross-Border and Private Equity Competition**
UK financial services firms are experiencing particularly pronounced competitive tension, with overseas acquirers increasingly recognizing the value opportunity presented by high-quality UK-listed businesses. Private equity buyers are also driving significant activity in the sector.

**Sector-Specific M&A Activity**
Public M&A activity has been particularly pronounced across financial services, industrials, and business services, with the broader picture showing significant demand for UK-listed businesses despite continued geopolitical uncertainty, a shifting macroeconomic backdrop, and the impact of inflation and interest rates.

## Nubank's Annual KPIs and 2023 Performance Against Company Priorities

### Key Performance Indicators (2023)

**Customer Growth**
- **93.9 million customers globally** by December 31, 2023
- Added **19.3 million customers year-over-year** (4.8 million in Q4 2023 alone)
- Positioned as one of the largest and fastest-growing digital financial services platforms worldwide, up from 54 million customers just two years prior

**Revenue**
- **Over $8 billion in total revenues** for full-year 2023
- **$2.4 billion** in Q4 2023 quarterly revenue

**Profitability**
- **First full-year net profit exceeding $1 billion** — a landmark achievement
- **$360.9 million** net income in Q4 2023
- **Annualized ROE of 23%** (compared to $58 million in Q4 2022)

**Monetization & Efficiency**
- **Monthly Average Revenue per Active Customer (ARPAC):** $10.6 in Q4 2023, growing steadily throughout the year
- **Cost to serve per active customer:** ~$0.9/month, remaining stable and among the lowest in the industry
- **Cost-to-income (efficiency) ratio:** 36.0% for Q4 2023 and full-year 2023, an improvement of **19 percentage points** versus full-year 2022, reinforcing Nu's position as one of the most efficient financial companies in Latin America

### Company Priorities for 2023 and Performance

**1. Expanding the Lending Book**
- Became the **third-largest lender in Brazil by number of customers with loans**
- Focused on both secured and unsecured credit expansion
- Credit penetration reached 53% of clients

**2. Deepening Customer Engagement and Cross-Selling**
- Successfully drove ARPAC growth to $10.6 per month
- Expanded financial products including personal loans, insurance, and investments
- Over 58% of monthly active customers who have been with Nu for over a year consider it their primary banking relationship

**3. Geographic Expansion**
- Continued dominance in Brazil with 70.9 million customers (including 2.5 million SMEs)
- Expanded into Mexico with 3.2 million customers
- Grew presence in Colombia with 565,000 customers

**4. Maintaining a Low-Cost Operating Platform**
- Successfully held cost-to-serve near $0.9 per active customer while scaling
- Achieved 36% efficiency ratio, improving 19 percentage points year-over-year

### Summary

Nubank's 2023 results demonstrated the effectiveness of its business model against all stated company priorities. {"content":"## Nubank (Nu Holdings) — Full-Year 2023 Key Performance Indicators

### Customer Growth
- **93.9 million customers globally** by December 31, 2023, adding **19.3 million customers year-over-year** (4.8 million in Q4 2023 alone).
- This positioned Nu as one of the largest and fastest-growing digital financial services platforms worldwide, up from 54 million customers just two years prior.

### Revenue
- **Over $8 billion in total revenues** for full-year 2023.
- Q4 2023 quarterly revenue reached **$2.4 billion**.

### Profitability
- **First full-year net profit exceeding $1 billion** — a landmark achievement.
- Q4 2023 net income was **$360.9 million**, with an annualized **ROE of 23%**, compared to $58 million in Q4 2022.

### Monetization & Efficiency
- **Monthly Average Revenue per Active Customer (ARPAC):** $10.6 in Q4 2023, growing steadily throughout the year.
- **Cost to serve per active customer:** ~$0.9/month, remaining stable and among the lowest in the industry.
- **Cost-to-income (efficiency) ratio:** 36.0% for Q4 2023 and full-year 2023, an improvement of **19 percentage points** versus full-year 2022 — reinforcing Nu's position as one of the most efficient financial companies in Latin America.

### Company Priorities & Strategic Focus (2023)
- **Expanding the lending book** (both secured and unsecured credit), having become the third-largest lender in Brazil by number of customers with loans.
- **Deepening customer engagement and cross-selling** financial products (personal loans, insurance, investments) to drive ARPAC growth.
- **Geographic expansion** into Mexico and Colombia alongside continued dominance in Brazil.
- **Maintaining a low-cost operating platform** while scaling, with the cost-to-serve holding near $0.9 per active customer.

### Summary
Nubank's 2023 results demonstrated the effectiveness of its business model: rapid customer acquisition, rising monetization per user, and disciplined cost management combined to deliver the company's first billion-dollar annual profit on over $8 billion in revenue, with a 23% ROE and a 36% efficiency ratio.

### Customer Growth
- **93.9 million customers globally** by December 31, 2023, adding **19.3 million customers year-over-year** (4.8 million in Q4 2023 alone).
- This positioned Nu as one of the largest and fastest-growing digital financial services platforms worldwide, up from 54 million customers just two years prior.

### Revenue
- **Over $8 billion in total revenues** for full-year 2023.
- Q4 2023 quarterly revenue reached **$2.4 billion**.

### Profitability
- **First full-year net profit exceeding $1 billion** — a landmark achievement.
- Q4 2023 net income was **$360.9 million**, with an annualized **ROE of 23%**, compared to $58 million in Q4 2022.

### Monetization & Efficiency
- **Monthly Average Revenue per Active Customer (ARPAC):** $10.6 in Q4 2023, growing steadily throughout the year.
- **Cost to serve per active customer:** ~$0.9/month, remaining stable and among the lowest in the industry.
- **Cost-to-income (efficiency) ratio:** 36.0% for Q4 2023 and full-year 2023, an improvement of **19 percentage points** versus full-year 2022 — reinforcing Nu's position as one of the most efficient financial companies in Latin America.

### Company Priorities & Strategic Focus (2023)
- **Expanding the lending book** (both secured and unsecured credit), having become the third-largest lender in Brazil by number of customers with loans.
- **Deepening customer engagement and cross-selling** financial products (personal loans, insurance, investments) to drive ARPAC growth.
- **Geographic expansion** into Mexico and Colombia alongside continued dominance in Brazil.
- **Maintaining a low-cost operating platform** while scaling, with the cost-to-serve holding near $0.9 per active customer.

### Summary
Nubank's 2023 results demonstrated the effectiveness of its business model: rapid customer acquisition, rising monetization per user, and disciplined cost management combined to deliver the company's first billion-dollar annual profit on over $8 billion in revenue, with a 23% ROE and a 36% efficiency ratio.

- **Cost-to-income (efficiency) ratio:** 36.0% for Q4 2023 and full-year 2023, an improvement of **19 percentage points** versus full-year 2022, reinforcing Nu's position as one of the most efficient financial companies in Latin America

### Company Priorities for 2023 and Performance

**1. Expanding the Lending Book**

**2. Deepening Customer Engagement and Cross-Selling**
- Successfully drove ARPAC growth to $10.6 per month
- Expanded financial products including personal loans, insurance, and investments
- Over 58% of monthly active customers who have been with Nu for over a year consider it their primary banking relationship

**3. Geographic Expansion**
- Continued dominance in Brazil with 70.9 million customers (including 2.5 million SMEs)
- Expanded into Mexico with 3.2 million customers
- Grew presence in Colombia with 565,000 customers

**4. Maintaining a Low-Cost Operating Platform**
- Successfully held cost-to-serve near $0.9 per active customer while scaling
- Achieved 36% efficiency ratio, improving 19 percentage points year-over-year

### Summary

Nubank's 2023 results demonstrated the effectiveness of its business model against all stated company priorities. The company achieved rapid customer acquisition, rising monetization per user, and disciplined cost management, which combined to deliver the company's first billion-dollar annual profit on over $8 billion in revenue, with a 23% ROE and a 36% efficiency ratio.

answer:
## N26 Products and Account Features

N26, the German digital bank founded in 2013 and headquartered in Berlin, offers a comprehensive range of products and account features across multiple tiers and has recently expanded its product portfolio significantly.

---

### Account Tiers

#### 1. **N26 Standard** (Free)
- No opening or maintenance fees
- Virtual Mastercard debit card (usable via Apple Pay and Google Pay)
- SEPA Instant Credit transfers at no extra cost
- Real-time spending notifications
- Basic budgeting and finance management tools

#### 2. **N26 Smart** (€4.90/month)
- Physical Mastercard debit card (choice of five colors)
- Up to 6 virtual cards
- 3 free domestic ATM withdrawals per month
- Up to 10 **Spaces** sub-accounts (with their own IBANs) for budgeting, savings goals, and direct debits
- **Shared Spaces** — manage funds together with up to 10 other N26 customers
- Link a virtual card to a Space to spend directly from it
- **Instant Savings** account with flexible access
- Automatic **Rules** to sort money into sub-accounts
- Round-ups and Income Sorter features

#### 3. **N26 Go** (€9.90/month)
- All Smart features, plus:
- **Travel insurance** (provided by Allianz) — covers trip cancellation, trip interruption, travel delay, baggage delay/loss, emergency medical & transportation, and personal liability while travelling (up to €10,000 for cancellation/rebooking fees)
- No foreign transaction fees on payments abroad
- Free international ATM withdrawals
- 5 free trades per month for Stocks & ETFs

#### 4. **N26 Metal** (€16.90/month)
- All Go features, plus:
- Premium heavyweight **metal card** in multiple colors/finishes
- Enhanced travel insurance (including pandemic/epidemic coverage via Allianz), mobile phone protection, and purchase protection
- Coverage extends to spouse/cohabitant and children (up to age 25 if in education) for travel covers
- Personal liability while travelling up to €500,000
- Unlimited free ATM withdrawals worldwide
- No markup on foreign exchange rates for card purchases and withdrawals
- 10 free trades per month for Stocks & ETFs
- Up to **4% interest** on Instant Savings
- Priority customer support
- Exclusive partner offers

---

### Business Accounts

N26 offers **Business Standard**, **Business Smart**, **Business Go**, and **Business Metal** accounts for freelancers and self-employed individuals, mirroring the personal tiers with added business features such as:
- 0.1% cashback on card purchases (Business Go)
- Automatic transaction categorization via AI
- Free monthly stock/ETF trades (Business Go and Business Metal)
- Accounting and invoicing tools (in development)
- A new **Small & Medium Business account** is also being rolled out for companies (sole proprietorships, UG, GmbH, AG) with up to 9 employees and max €2 million annual turnover, offering up to 0.5% cashback and free eurozone ATM withdrawals

---

### Key Features Across All Accounts

| Feature | Details |
|---|---|
| **Stocks & ETFs** | Buy and sell 4,000+ stocks, ETFs, and ETCs directly in the app for a flat €0.90 per trade (powered by Upvest). Fractional investing and savings plans available. Free trades included with Go (3/month), Metal (10/month). |
| **Crypto** | Crypto portfolio management within the app |
| **Instant Savings** | Flexible savings account with interest; rates vary by tier (up to 4% for Metal) |
| **Spaces** | Sub-accounts with individual IBANs for budgeting and goal-setting (up to 10 with Smart and above) |
| **Joint Accounts** | Shared account functionality |
| **Real-time notifications** | Push alerts for every transaction |
| **Mobile payments** | Apple Pay and Google Pay support |
| **SEPA transfers** | Instant incoming SEPA Credit transfers at no extra cost |
| **International transfers** | Send money abroad from the app |
| **Security** | Mastercard SecureCode, biometric login, card lock/unlock in-app |

---

### New Products and Features Launched in 2024-2025

#### **2024 Launches:**

1. **N26 Stocks & ETFs (January 2024)**
   - Launched in partnership with Upvest
   - Customers can buy and sell fractional shares of European and US assets at a fixed fee of €0.90 per trade
   - Initially rolled out in Austria, then expanded to Germany, Ireland, and other markets
   - Offers over 500 European and US stocks
   - Fee-free savings plans introduced
   - Free monthly trades for N26 You and N26 Metal members
   - Access to free Investment Plans

2. **N26 Crypto — France (March 2024)**
   - Launched cryptocurrency trading product in France
   - Allows customers to trade over 200 cryptocurrencies directly in the N26 app
   - Developed in partnership with Bitpanda GmbH
   - N26 Metal customers benefit from lower transaction fees (1% on Bitcoin, 2% on other coins)
   - Standard customers pay 1.5% on Bitcoin and 2.5% on other coins

3. **N26 Crypto — Germany, Switzerland, Belgium, Portugal & Ireland (2024)**
   - Expanded crypto trading to additional European markets
   - Offers nearly 200 coins
   - Same tiered pricing structure as France launch

4. **Updated Insurance Services (2024)**
   - Enhanced insurance for 'You' and 'Metal' personal and business account holders
   - Travel delays now covered after just 2 hours (down from 4)
   - Baggage delays covered after 4 hours (down from 12)
   - Personal liability coverage increased to €500,000 per trip
   - Coverage still includes baggage and travel delays up to €500, baggage theft up to €2,000, medical emergencies up to €1 million, and trip cancellations/interruptions up to €10,000

5. **N26 Instant Savings — Spain**
   - Launched Instant Savings account in Spain
   - Offers Spanish IBAN with 2.26% AER on deposits
   - No minimum deposit required
   - No conditions of permanence
   - No additional fees
   - Maximum balance of €50,000 for earning interest

6. **Instant Savings Expansion to 13 European Countries**
   - Extended instant savings accounts to 13 European countries
   - Broadened access to interest-bearing savings across customer base

#### **2025 Performance:**

- N26 reached its first full-year net profit in 2025 (€1.6 million net income)
- Revenue grew 13% to €501.6 million (from €445.4 million in 2024)
- Fee and commission income grew 21% to €184.2 million
- Net interest income grew 49% to €166.3 million
- Processes over €140 billion in transactions annually
- Serves customers in 24 European markets

---

N26's product strategy in 2024-2025 focused on transforming from a pure digital bank into a broader financial platform, adding investing (stocks, ETFs), crypto trading, enhanced insurance, and competitive savings products — all integrated within a single mobile app.

## N26 — Products and Account Features

N26 is a German fintech and digital bank headquartered in Berlin, founded in 2013. It operates across multiple European markets and offers a fully mobile, 100% digital banking experience via its app and web platform. Below is an overview of its account tiers and key features.

---

### Account Tiers

#### 1. **N26 Standard** (Free)
- No opening or maintenance fees
- Virtual Mastercard debit card (usable via Apple Pay and Google Pay)
- SEPA Instant Credit transfers at no extra cost
- Real-time spending notifications
- Basic budgeting and finance management tools

#### 2. **N26 Smart** (€4.90/month)
- Physical Mastercard debit card (choice of five colors)
- Up to 6 virtual cards
- 3 free domestic ATM withdrawals per month
- Up to 10 **Spaces** sub-accounts (with their own IBANs) for budgeting, savings goals, and direct debits
- **Shared Spaces** — manage funds together with up to 10 other N26 customers
- Link a virtual card to a Space to spend directly from it
- **Instant Savings** account with flexible access
- Automatic **Rules** to sort money into sub-accounts
- Round-ups and Income Sorter features

#### 3. **N26 Go** (€9.90/month)
- All Smart features, plus:
- **Travel insurance** (provided by Allianz) — covers trip cancellation, trip interruption, travel delay, baggage delay/loss, emergency medical & transportation, and personal liability while travelling (up to €10,000 for cancellation/rebooking fees)
- No foreign transaction fees on payments abroad
- Free international ATM withdrawals
- 5 free trades per month for Stocks & ETFs

#### 4. **N26 Metal** (€16.90/month)
- All Go features, plus:
- Premium heavyweight **metal card** in multiple colors/finishes
- Enhanced travel insurance (including pandemic/epidemic coverage via Allianz), mobile phone protection, and purchase protection
- Coverage extends to spouse/cohabitant and children (up to age 25 if in education) for travel covers
- Personal liability while travelling up to €500,000
- Unlimited free ATM withdrawals worldwide
- No markup on foreign exchange rates for card purchases and withdrawals
- 10 free trades per month for Stocks & ETFs
- Up to **4% interest** on Instant Savings
- Priority customer support
- Exclusive partner offers

---

### Business Accounts

N26 also offers **Business Standard**, **Business Smart**, **Business Go**, and **Business Metal** accounts for freelancers and self-employed individuals, mirroring the personal tiers with added business features such as:
- 0.1% cashback on card purchases (Business Go)
- Automatic transaction categorization via AI
- Free monthly stock/ETF trades (Business Go and Business Metal)
- Accounting and invoicing tools (in development)
- A new **Small & Medium Business account** is also being rolled out for companies (sole proprietorships, UG, GmbH, AG) with up to 9 employees and max €2 million annual turnover, offering up to 0.5% cashback and free eurozone ATM withdrawals.

---

### Key Features Across All Accounts

| Feature | Details |
|---|---|
| **Stocks & ETFs** | Buy and sell 4,000+ stocks, ETFs, and ETCs directly in the app for a flat €0.90 per trade (powered by Upvest). Fractional investing and savings plans available. Free trades included with Go (3/month), Metal (10/month). |
| **Crypto** | Crypto portfolio management within the app |
| **Instant Savings** | Flexible savings account with interest; rates vary by tier (up to 4% for Metal) |
| **Spaces** | Sub-accounts with individual IBANs for budgeting and goal-setting (up to 10 with Smart and above) |
| **Joint Accounts** | Shared account functionality |
| **Real-time notifications** | Push alerts for every transaction |
| **Mobile payments** | Apple Pay and Google Pay support |
| **SEPA transfers** | Instant incoming SEPA Credit transfers at no extra cost |
| **International transfers** | Send money abroad from the app |
| **Security** | Mastercard SecureCode, biometric login, card lock/unlock in-app |

explainability.content: N26 is a German fintech and digital bank founded in 2013, headquartered in Berlin, providing a fully digital banking experience.
The free N26 Standard account has no opening or maintenance fees, offers a virtual Mastercard usable via Apple Pay and Google Pay, and supports SEPA Instant Credit transfers at no extra cost.

N26 Smart, priced at €4.90 per month, includes a physical Mastercard debit card, up to six virtual cards, three free domestic ATM withdrawals, and allows creation of up to 10 Spaces sub‑accounts with individual IBANs for budgeting and savings.
N26 Go adds travel insurance (provided by Allianz), eliminates foreign transaction fees, provides free international ATM withdrawals, and includes three free stock/ETF trades per month.

N26 Metal, costing €16.90 per month, includes all Go benefits plus a premium metal card, enhanced travel insurance covering spouse/cohabitant and children up to age 25, unlimited free ATM withdrawals worldwide, no FX markup, ten free stock/ETF trades per month, and up to 4 % interest on Instant Savings.

Business account tiers (Standard, Smart, Go, Metal) mirror the personal tiers and add features such as 0.1 % cashback on purchases, AI‑driven transaction categorisation, free monthly stock/ETF trades, and are available for freelancers, self‑employed, and small‑medium enterprises with up to 9 employees and €2 million turnover.

{"content":"## N26 — New Product Launches in 2024 and 2025

### 2024

1. **N26 Stocks & ETFs (January 2024)**
   N26 launched a stock and ETF trading product in partnership with Upvest. Customers can buy and sell fractional shares of European and US assets at a fixed fee of €0.90 per trade. The product initially rolled out in Austria, with plans to expand to Germany and other markets. Fee-free savings plans were also announced for the following months.

2. **N26 Crypto — France (March 2024)**
   N26 launched its cryptocurrency trading product, N26 Crypto, in France. The product allows customers to trade over 200 cryptocurrencies directly in the N26 app, developed in partnership with Bitpanda GmbH.

3. **N26 Crypto — Germany, Switzerland, Belgium, Portugal & Ireland (2024)**
   Following the initial launch in Austria, N26 Crypto expanded to Germany, Switzerland, Belgium, Portugal, and Ireland, offering nearly 200 coins. N26 Metal customers benefit from lower transaction fees (1% on Bitcoin, 2% on other coins), while standard customers pay 1.5% on Bitcoin and 2.5% on other coins.

4. **N26 Stocks & ETFs — Ireland (2024)**
   N26 expanded its stock and ETF trading product to Ireland, offering over 500 European and US stocks, with free monthly trades for N26 You and N26 Metal members and access to free Investment Plans.

5. **Updated Insurance Services (2024)**
   N26 launched enhanced insurance services for 'You' and 'Metal' personal and business account holders. Travel insurance was improved — travel delays covered after just 2 hours (down from 4), baggage delays after 4 hours (down from 12), and personal liability coverage up to €500,000 per trip.

6. **N26 Instant Savings — Spain**
   N26 launched its Instant Savings account in Spain, offering eligible customers a Spanish IBAN with 2.26% AER on deposits, no minimum deposit, no conditions of permanence, and no additional fees.

7. **Instant Savings Expansion to 13 European Countries**
   N26 extended its instant savings accounts to 13 European countries, broadening access to interest-bearing savings across its customer base.

### 2025

8. **Continued Revenue & Product Growth**
   N26 reached its first full-year net profit in 2025 (€1.6 million net income on €501.6 million revenue, up 13% from €445.4 million in 2024). Fee and commission income grew 21% to €184.2 million, and net interest income grew 49% to €166.3 million — reflecting the impact of the expanded product suite (trading, crypto, savings, insurance) on the bank's revenue mix. N26 processes over €140 billion in transactions annually and serves customers in 24 European markets.

N26's product strategy in 2024–2025 focused on transforming from a pure digital bank into a broader financial platform, adding investing (stocks, ETFs), crypto trading, enhanced insurance, and competitive savings products — all integrated within a single mobile app.

## N26 — New Product Launches in 2024 and 2025

### 2024

1. **N26 Stocks & ETFs (January 2024)**
   N26 launched a stock and ETF trading product in partnership with Upvest. Customers can buy and sell fractional shares of European and US assets at a fixed fee of €0.90 per trade. The product initially rolled out in Austria, with plans to expand to Germany and other markets. Fee-free savings plans were also announced for the following months.

2. **N26 Crypto — France (March 2024)**
   N26 launched its cryptocurrency trading product, N26 Crypto, in France. The product allows customers to trade over 200 cryptocurrencies directly in the N26 app, developed in partnership with Bitpanda GmbH.

3. **N26 Crypto — Germany, Switzerland, Belgium, Portugal & Ireland (2024)**
   Following the initial launch in Austria, N26 Crypto expanded to Germany, Switzerland, Belgium, Portugal, and Ireland, offering nearly 200 coins. N26 Metal customers benefit from lower transaction fees (1% on Bitcoin, 2% on other coins), while standard customers pay 1.5% on Bitcoin and 2.5% on other coins.

4. **N26 Stocks & ETFs — Ireland (2024)**
   N26 expanded its stock and ETF trading product to Ireland, offering over 500 European and US stocks, with free monthly trades for N26 You and N26 Metal members and access to free Investment Plans.

5. **Updated Insurance Services (2024)**
   N26 launched enhanced insurance services for 'You' and 'Metal' personal and business account holders. Travel insurance was improved — travel delays covered after just 2 hours (down from 4), baggage delays after 4 hours (down from 12), and personal liability coverage up to €500,000 per trip.

6. **N26 Instant Savings — Spain**
   N26 launched its Instant Savings account in Spain, offering eligible customers a Spanish IBAN with 2.26% AER on deposits, no minimum deposit, no conditions of permanence, and no additional fees.

7. **Instant Savings Expansion to 13 European Countries**
   N26 extended its instant savings accounts to 13 European countries, broadening access to interest-bearing savings across its customer base.

### 2025

8. **Continued Revenue & Product Growth**
   N26 reached its first full-year net profit in 2025 (€1.6 million net income on €501.6 million revenue, up 13% from €445.4 million in 2024). Fee and commission income grew 21% to €184.2 million, and net interest income grew 49% to €166.3 million — reflecting the impact of the expanded product suite (trading, crypto, savings, insurance) on the bank's revenue mix. N26 processes over €140 billion in transactions annually and serves customers in 24 European markets.

N26's product strategy in 2024–2025 focused on transforming from a pure digital bank into a broader financial platform, adding investing (stocks, ETFs), crypto trading, enhanced insurance, and competitive savings products — all integrated within a single mobile app.
